MIDTERMS — IT 105 DISCRETE STRUCTURES 1
Week 6 — Formal Proofs vs. Informal Proofs
The uploaded Midterm PPT covers Formal Proofs and Informal Proofs. Below is the full extraction of its educational content, preserving the PPT's terminology and explanations.

pages.source: User-provided exact content — Formal and Informal Proofs — page 2
pages.text:
1. FORMAL PROOFS VS INFORMAL PROOFS
The PPT introduces a comparison between:
	Formal Proofs
	Informal Proofs

pages.source: User-provided exact content — Formal and Informal Proofs — page 3
pages.text:
2. FORMAL PROOFS
What is Formal Proofs?
The PPT defines a proof as:
A proof is a precise, formal, and valid argument which establishes the truth of a statement.
A formal proof or derivation is a finite sequence of sentences called well-formed formulas in the case of a formal language.
The PPT also states:
Understanding how correct programs work is equivalent to proving theorems by induction.

pages.source: User-provided exact content — Formal and Informal Proofs — page 4
pages.text:
3. CHARACTERISTICS OF FORMAL PROOFS
The PPT presents five characteristics of formal proofs.

pages.source: User-provided exact content — Formal and Informal Proofs — page 5
pages.text:
3.1 Rigorous Structure
Formal proofs adhere to strict rules of logic and mathematical syntax.
They are often presented in a:
	Systematic
	Step-by-step
manner, following established proof techniques.
Key idea
Formal proofs follow established logical and mathematical rules rather than relying only on an explanation or intuition.

pages.source: User-provided exact content — Formal and Informal Proofs — page 6
pages.text:
3.2 Symbolic Language
Formal proofs frequently employ:
	Symbolic notation
	Logical symbols
	Mathematical symbols
to express ideas precisely.
They rely on the language of logic and mathematical symbols to convey the reasoning.
Key idea
Formal proofs use symbolic and mathematical notation to make the reasoning precise.

pages.source: User-provided exact content — Formal and Informal Proofs — page 7
pages.text:
3.3 Assumptions and Axioms
Formal proofs explicitly state the:
	Assumptions
	Axioms
used in the proof.
Every step in the proof is justified by previously established:
	Rules
	Definitions
	Axioms
	Theorems
Key idea
Each step must have a logical basis.

pages.source: User-provided exact content — Formal and Informal Proofs — page 8
pages.text:
3.4 No Ambiguity
Formal proofs leave no room for ambiguity.
Each step must be logically derived from the previous steps, and there should be no gaps in the reasoning.
Key idea
The reasoning must be explicit and complete.

pages.source: User-provided exact content — Formal and Informal Proofs — page 9
pages.text:
3.5 Verification
Formal proofs can be mechanically verified by computers or by humans.
They provide a high level of confidence in the validity of the argument.
Key idea
A formal proof can be checked systematically to verify whether its reasoning is valid.

pages.source: User-provided exact content — Formal and Informal Proofs — page 10
pages.text:
4. INFORMAL PROOFS
What is Informal Proofs?
The PPT states:
An informal proofs are arguments that depend on their matter as well as their logical form.
It further explains:
The steps of the proofs are not expressed in any formal language as e.g. propositional logic

pages.source: User-provided exact content — Formal and Informal Proofs — page 11
pages.text:
5. CHARACTERISTICS OF INFORMAL PROOFS
The PPT presents five characteristics of informal proofs.

pages.source: User-provided exact content — Formal and Informal Proofs — page 12
pages.text:
5.1 Natural Language
Informal proofs are typically presented in everyday language, without strict adherence to:
	Symbolic notation
	Formal logic
They aim to explain the reasoning in a way that is accessible to a wide audience.
Key idea
Informal proofs primarily use ordinary language to communicate the reasoning.

pages.source: User-provided exact content — Formal and Informal Proofs — page 13
pages.text:
5.2 Less Structured
Informal proofs may lack the strict structure of formal proofs.
They often rely on:
	Narrative explanations
	Examples
	Intuitive reasoning
to convey the argument's validity.
Key idea
Informal proofs do not necessarily follow a rigid step-by-step formal structure.

pages.source: User-provided exact content — Formal and Informal Proofs — page 14
pages.text:
5.3 Emphasis on Understanding
Informal proofs focus on conveying the underlying ideas and concepts behind the argument.
They may prioritize:
	Intuition
	Insight
over rigorous formalism.
Key idea
The goal is to help the reader understand why the argument works.

pages.source: User-provided exact content — Formal and Informal Proofs — page 15
pages.text:
5.4 Flexibility
Informal proofs allow for more flexibility in presentation style.
They may include:
	Diagrams
	Examples
	Analogies
	Other illustrative techniques
to aid in understanding.
Key idea
The proof can use different ways of explaining an idea as long as the reasoning is communicated.

pages.source: User-provided exact content — Formal and Informal Proofs — page 16
pages.text:
5.5 Subjectivity
Informal proofs may be subject to:
	Interpretation
	The reader's understanding
	The reader's judgment
They may not provide the same level of certainty as formal proofs but can still convey convincing arguments.
Key idea
Because informal proofs rely more on natural language and interpretation, the reader's understanding can affect how the argument is perceived.

pages.source: User-provided exact content — Formal and Informal Proofs — page 17
pages.text:
6. FORMAL VS. INFORMAL PROOFS — COMPLETE COMPARISON
Aspect	Formal Proofs	Informal Proofs
Language	Symbolic notation, logical symbols, mathematical symbols	Natural/everyday language
Structure	Rigorous and systematic	Less structured
Reasoning	Every step is logically derived and justified	May rely on narrative explanations and intuitive reasoning
Assumptions/Axioms	Explicitly stated	Not necessarily expressed formally
Ambiguity	No room for ambiguity	May be subject to interpretation
Understanding	Emphasizes rigorous formalism	Emphasizes underlying ideas, intuition, and insight
Presentation	Strict proof techniques	Flexible presentation

pages.source: User-provided exact content — Formal and Informal Proofs — page 18
pages.text:
Examples/Illustrations	Primarily formal logical/mathematical notation	Can use diagrams, examples, analogies, etc.
Verification	Can be mechanically verified by computers or humans	Relies more on reader's understanding and judgment
Certainty	Provides a high level of confidence in validity	May not provide the same level of certainty but can still convey convincing arguments
This comparison is assembled directly from the characteristics presented across the two sections of the PPT.

FORMAL PROOFS
Definition
A proof is a precise, formal, and valid argument that establishes the truth of a statement.
A formal proof or derivation is a finite sequence of sentences called well-formed formulas in a formal language.
Five characteristics
	Rigorous Structure
	Symbolic Language
	Assumptions and Axioms
	No Ambiguity
	Verification

INFORMAL PROOFS
Definition
Informal proofs are arguments that depend on their matter as well as their logical form.
Their steps are not expressed in a formal language such as propositional logic.
Five characteristics
